text:
Besides, money had never been spared at the Castle; the sums were always large there. What, for example, did a dinner like that not cost! But now it was to look empty everywhere, even in the lady of the Castle’s familiar jewel case, and therefore the son-in-law’s money was to restore the splendour.

How much does he have, one wonders?

Oh, fie, he has such an unfathomable amount of money.

Johannes rose again and went down into the garden. The lilacs were in bloom; streams of fragrance from auriculas and narcissi, jasmines and lilies of the valley met him. He sought out a corner down by the wall and sat on a stone; a thicket concealed him from all the world. He was exhausted by emotion, weary as a slave, his reason darkened; he thought of getting up and going home, but remained sitting there, dull and listless. Then he heard murmuring farther along the gravel path; someone was coming, and he recognized Victoria’s voice. He held his breath and waited a little; then the lieutenant’s uniform also flashed through the foliage. The betrothed couple were walking together.

I do not think, he said, that this quite adds up. You listen to what he says, you sit there concerning yourself with his speech and cry out. What did that really mean?

She stopped and stood tall before him.

Do you want to know? she said.

Yes.

She was silent.

It is all the same to me if it meant nothing, he continued. Then you need not say it.

She subsided again.

No, it meant nothing, she replied.

They began walking again. The lieutenant nervously shrugged his epaulettes and said loudly:

He ought to watch himself a little. Otherwise an officer’s hand might box his ears.

They took the path to the summerhouse.

Johannes remained sitting on the stone for a while, dull and tormented as before. Everything was beginning to be a matter of indifference to him. The lieutenant had grown suspicious of him, and his fiancée had given an account of herself on the spot. She said what had to be said, set the officer’s heart at rest, and walked on with him. And the starlings chattered in the branches above their heads. Indeed. May God grant them a long life.... He had spoken on her behalf at dinner and torn out his heart; it had cost him dearly to put right and cover over her insolent interruption, and she had not thanked him for it. She had seized her glass and drunk. Cheers, look at me, how prettily I drink.... For that matter, look at a woman from the side when she drinks. Let her drink from a cup, from a glass, from anything at all, but look at her from the side. She puts on such airs that it is dreadful. She purses her mouth and dips its outermost rim into the drink, and she is in despair if, while she does so, anyone notices her hand. On the whole, do not look at a woman’s hand. She cannot bear it; she capitulates. At once she begins drawing her hand back, placing it in an ever more beautiful position, all to conceal a wrinkle, a crookedness in the fingers, or a less well-shaped nail. In the end she can bear it no longer, but asks, beside herself: what are you looking at?.... She had once kissed him, once, one summer. It was so long ago; God knows whether it had even been true. How was it—had they not been sitting on a bench? They talked together for a long time, and when they left he came so very close to her that he touched her arm. Outside an entrance she kissed him. I love you! she said.... Now they had passed by; perhaps they were still sitting in the summerhouse. The lieutenant would box his ears, he had said. He had heard it perfectly well; he was not asleep, but neither did he rise and step forward. An officer’s hand, he had said. Indeed, it was a matter of indifference to him....

He rose from the stone and followed them to the summerhouse. It was empty. Up by the veranda of the main building, Camilla stood calling to him; would he please come, there was coffee in the garden room. He followed her. The betrothed couple were sitting in the garden room; several others were present as well. He was given his coffee, stepped back, and found himself a place.

Camilla began talking to him. Her face was so bright, and she looked at him with open eyes; he could not resist her, he joined in the conversation, answered her questions, and laughed. Where had he been? In the garden? That was not true at all; she had searched in the garden and had not found him. Far from it, he had not been in the garden.

Was he in the garden, Victoria? she asked.

Victoria replied:

No, I did not see him.

The lieutenant cast her an embittered glance and, to give his fiancée a warning, said unnecessarily loudly across to the landowner:

Was it the case that you wished to take me woodcock shooting at your estate?

Yes indeed, the landowner replied. You are welcome.

The lieutenant looked at Victoria. She said nothing and remained sitting as before, making no effort whatever to dissuade him from this woodcock shoot at the landowner’s estate. His face grew darker and darker; he stroked his moustache with nervous movements.

Camilla addressed another question to Victoria.

Then the lieutenant rose with a sudden movement and said to the landowner:

Very well, then I shall go with you tonight, at once.

With that he left the room.

The landowner and some others followed.

There was a brief pause.

Suddenly the door opened and the lieutenant entered again. He was in a state of extreme agitation.

Have you forgotten something? Victoria asked, rising.

He took a few bounding steps by the door, as though unable to stand still, and went straight over to Johannes, whom, as if in passing, he struck with his hand. Then he ran back to the door and continued hopping about.

Take care, man, you struck me in the eye, Johannes said, laughing hollowly.

You are mistaken, the lieutenant replied. I boxed your ear. Do you understand? Do you understand?

Johannes reached for his handkerchief, wiped his eye, and said:

You do not mean that. You know I can fold you double and put you in my pocket.

At that same moment he rose.

Then the lieutenant hastily opened the door and stepped outside.

I do mean it! he shouted back. I mean it, you nag!

Then he slammed the door with a crash.

Johannes sat down again.

Victoria was still standing approximately in the middle of the floor. She looked at him and was pale as a corpse.

Did he strike you? Camilla asked in the greatest astonishment.

By accident. He caught me in the eye. Would you like to see?

God, it is red; there is blood. No, do not rub it; let me pour water on it. Your handkerchief is so coarse—here, take it back; I shall use my own. Did anyone ever see the like, right in the eye!

Victoria also held out her handkerchief. She said nothing. Then she walked very slowly to the glass door, where she remained standing with her back to the room, looking out. She tore her handkerchief into small strips. A few minutes later she opened the door and left the garden room, silent and mute.
